intro: The framework was designed for the nonhospital organization, the target center defined in Chapter 3, whose conditions set the minimum implementation level, but hospitals hosted 239 of the 347 site records in the registry sample (68.9%), so a framework that fitted only the target center would leave out most of the settings where these investigations take place. The scalability model answers DR12, which asks that the depth of implementation follow the resources of the center and the risk of the investigation while the documentation trail stays complete and consistent at every depth. Scaling to the risk of the investigation applies the proportionality that ICH E6(R3) asks of quality management [6]. Scaling to the resources of the site is a choice of this design, and it can hold only because the documentation trail does not scale. What scales is the number of instruments in use, and each instrument keeps the same form at every level. The three implementation levels follow the organizational environments of Table 3.3, according to what the framework can assume stands behind the site, and the risk of each investigation adds instruments within each level.
body: The framework can scale because each of its instruments describes a control function, as the overview of this chapter set out, so a function that a site does not yet run as a separate instrument can be covered by another record that the site already keeps. Each level therefore has a recommended minimum set of instruments, twelve for a nonhospital organization, eighteen for a nonacademic hospital, and all twenty-four for an academic organization, and each instrument left out has a proxy, another record that the site keeps and that takes on its function, named in Table 4.2. The minimum is a recommendation, so a site at any level that can run more instruments should run them, all twenty-four where it can.

The minimum level is that of the target center, where no hospital system or university stands behind the site and the clinical staff carry the research work. Its twelve instruments cover the duties that the site already holds and give each gap at least one answer. Oversight, delegation, training, and the credentialing of surgeons rest on the POT, the RACI, the TRE, and the SCR, the risk register opens before the first participant, and every safety case is followed in the SART. The eligibility decision, the record of each procedure, and the log of each image set are kept, internal verification runs through its checklist, follow-up is reviewed in the FUCR, and the lessons of the investigation are drawn in the PIDLR. The six functions may be held by few people, each with a named substitute, so the accumulation does not leave a CtQ function dependent on one individual, and where the separation that DR10 asks for cannot be complete, the operational constraint prevails, as Section 3.5 established. Review is never done by the person who did the work, and it never falls below the cadence that the pillars fixed, such as the monthly review of safety cases.

In a nonacademic hospital, the hospital system stands behind the site, with services such as radiology and controlled storage that the site can use, and more people can share the work of review. The recommended minimum rises to eighteen instruments. The six added are those that need time for analysis and planning, the learning curve log, the complication log with its signal review, the plan for internal verification, the indicators, and the corrective action log, and with them every gap in Table 3.1 has its full answer.

In an academic organization, a university stands behind the hospital, and the site may already have a research unit and an institutional quality system. All twenty-four instruments are recommended, and the six added at this level give formal structure to larger teams, from the graded delegation matrix and the milestone review log to the training requirements matrix and the site’s own records of imaging readiness, screening, and visits. The framework does not replace an institutional system. Where the institution already keeps training records or a system for corrective action, the instruments refer to them, as DR11 asks, and the CtQ domains and surgical instruments add what such a system was not built to hold, the conduct of the site at the level of the named surgeon, device, and investigation. Infrastructure of this kind still has to be built and measured, and clinical trial units differ in the services they provide [89, 90].

The categories of Table 3.3 describe what kind of organization a site is and say little about how it is prepared for research. In one survey, stakeholders from higher-level hospitals performed better on average, but substantial room for improvement remained [88], and Section 3.4.4 showed that shortages of staff and infrastructure are also reported in hospitals and academic centers. The level therefore states what the framework can assume. A site that lacks the support its category assumes runs the set of the level below, and a nonhospital organization with research capacity of its own can run the set of a higher one. The PI records the level at the review that closes start-up and revisits it when the capacity of the site changes during conduct, for example when the person who coordinates the investigation leaves. Revisiting the level in this way resembles the repeated institutional self-assessment that has been associated with better capability to conduct research, although that association could not be shown to be causal [30].

Within each level, the risk of the investigation adds instruments, domain by domain, where the risk register rates a domain as high. Strong operator dependence, as with a new implant design or surgical technique, calls for the learning curve log, limited classification reliability calls for the imaging and training controls of the higher levels, and the operational weight of a long follow-up calls for closer review of retention. A nonhospital site that implants a new design therefore adds the learning curve log to its twelve instruments. Where the risk calls for more than the site can run, the site draws on the support of the sponsor, such as proctoring, or declines the investigation at feasibility.

What does not scale is the evidence that the investigation was conducted as required. The MDR requires all investigation information to be recorded, handled, and stored so that it can be accurately reported, interpreted, and verified, and it requires Member States to inspect investigation sites at an appropriate level [10]. A site at the minimum level is therefore protected only as far as its records remain complete, consistent, current, and retrievable. These records, from consent, delegation, and training to the accountability of each implanted unit, deviations, adverse events, and source documents, are required by ISO 14155:2026 and the MDR whatever the level [8, 10], so they stay the same at every level and at every degree of risk, and the framework only fixes where each one sits. The instruments in use also keep their rules at every level, so the risk register covers all twelve domains wherever it is kept, and the record of each procedure is made in the operating room.
